I did a research paper in high school on the whole dispute. What's so funny to this day, is that if you asked people in 1989 on the likelihood of a certain Eastern European country reunifying with the West vs. a group of islands being transferred to another country, people would have sworn the latter would occur first and yet, it's been 27 years since a significant historical event.

Going back on-topic, the reason why the island nation wants a formal peace treaty with its northern neighbor to end World War II is due to an agreement both countries made in 1956. The 1956 Joint Declaration states that if a peace treaty were to be signed, certain islands will remain under the northern neighbor's sovereignty while others will be under the island nation's control. So in essence, the framework of splitting the four disputed islands is already in place. However, there have been a couple of factors on both sides of why the dispute is still a big problem.

Reasons why the island nation did not/couldn't accept the 1956 joint agreement:

* By accepting a peace treaty, the island nation will automatically lose any future claim to certain islands.
* A large country intervened in the original deal, stating that if the island nation concedes to giving up the islands then it should lay claim to another territory, which was already occupied at the time by the large country.
* The large country's foreign policy at the time was a policy of containment against the threat of Communism, and any resolution of conflict between the island nation and the northern neighbor would be detrimental to that policy. The island nation was seen as a bulwark against Communism as shown by the number of military bases and operations originating from there.
* The dispute to some nationalists in the island nation has been ongoing fuel for claiming the victimization of the country during WWII, being stabbed in the back by the breach of a neutrality pact, the seizure of the islands after a significant date in 1945, and POWs that were left behind in the northern neighbor.
* The ongoing dispute solidifies the need for a large country's presence, due to an ongoing threat of aggression from the northern neighbor.

Reasons why the northern neighbor did not/couldn't accept the 1956 joint agreement:

* The oceans around the islands are a strategic resource to the northern neighbor, with it separating two significant bodies of water. During the Cold War, nuclear submarines were stationed there to launch potential warheads against the large country.
* The ocean is rich in marine life, due to the islands being in a location where cold and warm currents meet.
* If the northern neighbor were to lose territories occupied at the end of WWII, the large country should also lose its claim of occupying another territory.
* If the northern neighbor "gives back" territories to the island nation, there could be a wave of demands from other countries in the region.
* Over two generations of citizens from the northern neighbor lived and died on the islands, with many buried on its soil.
* The islands are a matter of national pride and winning the war on the eastern front.
* There was still some distrust of the island nation, with a historical leader during WWII comparing a surprise attack in the early 20th century to a significant attack in 1941.

Better as in more "effective" per the regulatory requirements for clinical trials:

The organization performs a series of clinical trials in humans in three phases, which regulators monitor, to test if the drug is effective and safe.

The regulatory body doesn't review factors like cost, and pain to the patient is part of the risk-benefit analysis that shows their product is overall more safe and effective than conventional treatments. For example, a drug can be more painful than traditional treatment, but if it provides a more favorable prognosis and the duration is really short, it can be viewed as being "effective" while being safe.

The issue is that if a drug is not clearly shown to be more effective or safer than what's currently available. If the clinical trial shows that it's a mixed bag, it doesn't matter if the drug is significantly cheaper to produce, since cost is never a factor for regulatory approvals (although it is for certain healthcare programs for approved drugs). The regulatory body will usually not approve the drug, since existing modes of treatment are considered sufficient and you are adding new (unknown) risks to an existing patient population.

I work in medical device research and development, and you may not appreciate my perspective. 

Polycarbonate fittings, which are commonly used in surgical procedures, contain a specific chemical compound. There is currently no alternative method for synthesizing polycarbonate other than polymerizing this compound. Therefore, unless there is a ban on polycarbonate and a significant shift towards using glass and metal fittings that can withstand high pressures, these materials are unlikely to be phased out, even if it contradicts certain regulatory standards.

Blood bags and surgical tubing represent a different scenario. Both are typically made from plasticized PVC, which contains a specific plasticizer, and there are other less effective alternatives (like laminated low-density polyethylene and ethylene-vinyl acetate) as well as more costly options (thermoplastic polyurethane) that cannot truly match the gas and water permeability of PVC. Interestingly, the plasticizer actually aids in prolonging the storage life of blood, leading to recommendations from pharmacopoeias for the use of plasticized PVC in blood bags.

From my experience in the United States and what I have seen online, the standard wait is 2 weeks (14 days) if they are interested in you.

Although I've applied to companies in Japan in the past, I've never accepted any jobs and I've only been working in the US all my life. However, here are some thoughts.

First off, we are in June now and no company in the world (that is not a relative of yours) can give you with 100% certainty that there is a job in December. The hiring of prospective entry-level positions are the first positions on the chopping block when a company is going through financial difficulty, restructuring, or downsizing. I honestly wouldn't be surprised if your CEO tells you in November "sorry bud, the company is going through bad times" when he already knew that he will need to twist multiple arms to seriously hire you off-cycle.

Second, as others mentioned, the hiring process usually is in April of each year and companies in Japan usually do not do mid-year hires. If it is necessary, it would be a special case and you can expect an extra layer of bureaucracy if they are seriously interested in you. This is on top of usually a (1) physical resume drop-off at a booth at a conference/event, (2) surviving the in-person interview panel, and (3) waiting for the on-site interview (aka "Final Interview") where you actually meet your hiring manager and their boss. It sounds like you only finished Step 1, so if you don't hear anything back soon then you are either rejected or in the backup pile.

Lastly, a 2-week wait from my perspective is usually the tail-end of when a company in the US should have already made a decision on you or if they are just about to schedule a phone interview. Most online applications I made provide email responses within 2-8 days, and this is knowing in advance that I am within the top 10% of the application pool. If it takes more than 2 weeks, it usually means: (1) there are way too many applicants and you might not get your turn or pending, (2) your resume/application was filtered out, (3) your application is not competitive and in the backup pile.

Since you are in a special situation where you are waiting for a job in 6 months and would be a referral by your CEO, you will probably need to be patient. However, an inquiry every 2 weeks would probably not hurt to keep them aware that you haven't dropped your interest/application.
